questions.question: Under Linux CFS, a freshly woken task must be inserted into the runqueue and the next runnable task chosen without scanning every task. With N runnable tasks, what asymptotic cost does the red-black tree give per insertion or selection?
questions.explanation: CFS keys runnable tasks by vruntime in a red-black tree, so insertion, deletion, and fetching the leftmost (smallest-vruntime) node each cost O(log n).

questions.question: High-priority task H blocks on a mutex held by low-priority task L, while medium-priority task M keeps preempting L, so H starves. Which protocol temporarily raises L's priority to H's until the mutex is released?
questions.explanation: Priority inheritance lends the blocked higher priority to the lock holder, so L preempts M, finishes its critical section, and lets H proceed.

questions.question: Tasks of priorities 2, 5, and 9 (higher number = higher priority) may all lock semaphore S. Under the protocol that assigns each resource a ceiling equal to the highest priority of any task that may lock it, at what effective priority does the priority-2 task execute while holding S?
questions.explanation: The priority ceiling of S is 9, the maximum among its potential lockers. While the priority-2 task holds S it runs at priority 9, blocking out even the priority-5 task.

questions.question: Three ready periodic jobs have remaining execution times of 3, 5, and 2 ms and absolute deadlines at t = 50, t = 80, and t = 20 respectively. Under the dynamic-priority real-time algorithm, which job runs next?
questions.explanation: EDF always runs the ready job with the nearest absolute deadline regardless of its burst length, so the 2 ms job due at t = 20 is scheduled.

questions.question: Two periodic tasks are released together: task A has period 10 ms and task B has period 50 ms. Under rate-monotonic scheduling, which task is assigned the higher fixed priority?
questions.explanation: Rate-monotonic assigns priorities inversely to period length: the shorter period means a higher request rate, so A (10 ms) outranks B (50 ms).

questions.question: A real-time audio thread must run until it voluntarily blocks or a higher-priority task arrives; equal-priority peers must never timeslice it. Which Linux scheduling policy should it request?
questions.explanation: SCHED_FIFO is the first-in-first-out real-time class: a thread keeps the CPU until it blocks or is preempted by a strictly higher priority, unlike SCHED_RR which rotates equal-priority threads on a quantum.

questions.question: A compute job keeps migrating between CPU0 and CPU1 on every timeslice and suffers a burst of cache misses after each hop. What should the administrator set so the scheduler runs it only on CPU0?
questions.explanation: Setting the affinity mask (e.g., via sched_setaffinity or taskset) restricts the process to CPU0, preserving its warm cache instead of losing state on every migration.

questions.question: CPU0's runqueue is empty while CPU1's holds 12 runnable threads. Which mechanism lets the idle CPU0 pull runnable threads out of CPU1's runqueue?
questions.explanation: Work stealing (pull migration) is the pull side of load balancing: an idle CPU drains work from a busy peer's runqueue so both cores stay busy.

questions.question: A root administrator wants a critical batch daemon to get the highest CPU priority available to ordinary time-sharing processes on Linux. What nice value should be assigned to it?
questions.explanation: Nice values span -20 (highest priority) to +19 (lowest). Only root may set a negative value, so -20 gives the daemon maximum time-share priority.

questions.question: An interactive editor never finishes its time slice because it keeps blocking on keyboard input, while a compiler burns its whole quantum every round. Which scheduler keeps the editor in a high-priority queue while demoting the compiler?
questions.explanation: MLFQ demotes jobs that exhaust their quantum and retains priority for jobs that block early, automatically favoring I/O-bound interactive work over CPU-bound jobs.

questions.question: P1 arrives at 0 (burst 8), P2 at 1 (burst 4), P3 at 2 (burst 9), and P4 at 3 (burst 5). What is the average waiting time under preemptive SJF?
questions.explanation: SRTF runs P1, P2, P4, P1, P3, giving waits of 9, 0, 15, and 2. The average is 26/4 = 6.5 ms.

questions.question: Using the same arrivals (P1 at 0 burst 8, P2 at 1 burst 4, P3 at 2 burst 9, P4 at 3 burst 5), what is the average waiting time under non-preemptive SJF?
questions.explanation: Non-preemptive SJF runs P1, P2, P4, P3 with waits of 0, 7, 15, and 9. The average is 31/4 = 7.75 ms.

questions.question: P1 (burst 8), P2 (burst 4), and P3 (burst 6) all arrive at time 0. With Round Robin and quantum 4, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: RR executes P1, P2, P3, P1, P3 with completions at 16, 8, and 18. Waiting times are 8, 4, and 12, averaging 8 ms.

questions.question: With exponential averaging (alpha = 0.5), a last actual burst of 10, and a previous prediction of 12, what is the next predicted burst?
questions.explanation: τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1−α)·τ(n) = 0.5(10) + 0.5(12) = 11. Equal weighting simply averages the last burst and old prediction.

questions.question: As the number of tasks approaches infinity, what value does the rate-monotonic utilization bound approach?
questions.explanation: The RM bound n(2^(1/n) − 1) approaches ln 2 ≈ 0.693. Utilization below about 69% guarantees schedulability for large task sets.

questions.question: P1 arrives at 0 (burst 7), P2 at 2 (burst 4), P3 at 4 (burst 1), and P4 at 5 (burst 4). What is the average waiting time under preemptive SJF (SRTF)?
P1 arrives at 0 (burst 5), P2 at 1 (burst 3), and P3 at 2 (burst 8). With Round Robin and quantum 3, what is the average turnaround time?
An MLFQ has three queues: Q0 (quantum 4), Q1 (quantum 8), and Q2 (FCFS). A CPU-bound job with burst 20 arrives at time 0. How much of its burst remains when it first enters Q2?
questions.explanation: The job uses its full 4 ms in Q0 and 8 ms in Q1 before demotion: 20 - 4 - 8 = 8 ms left when it reaches FCFS Q2.

questions.question: Tasks T1 (period 20, exec 4), T2 (period 50, exec 15), and T3 (period 100, exec 30) have total utilization 0.80. Do they pass the rate-monotonic utilization-bound test for three tasks?
alternatives: It fails the RM bound test
questions.explanation: The RM bound for n=3 is 3(2^(1/3) - 1) = 0.78. Utilization 0.80 exceeds it, so the test is inconclusive and cannot guarantee schedulability.

questions.question: Under Linux CFS, task A has vruntime 500 ms and task B has vruntime 800 ms with equal nice values. Which task does CFS pick to run next?
questions.explanation: CFS always schedules the runnable task with the smallest vruntime, the leftmost node in its red-black tree.
